unit.why: A short halakhic report, cited from responsa, tells of the Shakh in Prague permitting grafted etrogim against his father-in-law's ruling, later regretting it, and a sign confirming the stricter ruling. These are non-Hasidic rabbinic figures.
unit.boundary_note: Division ends with a section heading ('סליק אות א ונתחיל אות ב') that belongs to the next section.

stories.summary_en: In Prague the Shakh's father-in-law disqualified grafted etrogim; powerful men persuaded the visiting Shakh to permit them; late in life he regretted it and asked forgiveness, and the etrog fell and its pitam broke as a sign.

quotes: והביאו אתרוגים מורכבים ופסק מורו וחמיו לפסלם
להתיר מטעם דשה אפי׳ מקצת שה
tags.why: The story turns on the legal validity of grafted etrogim.
The etrogim are ruled forbidden and the ruling is then overridden.
Powerful community members oppose the rabbi's ruling.
The Shakh regrets his ruling and asks forgiveness.

quotes: נפל לארץ ונשברה פטמותו והיה לאות
tags.why: The breaking of the etrog is a sign from Heaven.
The blessing over the etrog places the story at Sukkot.
The story vindicates a pre-Hasidic Prague rabbinic authority and is taken from an earlier responsa work.
The anecdote sits inside a halakhic citation frame.
The father-in-law of the Shakh is a central character.
